title: Pauri 1, meaning: joy, mother
hook: joy, mother, I have found the True Guru, easily, and the songs of joy are sung (Anand 1)
tomorrow: Stay with the Lord, my mind

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of pauri one, and your line, anand bhaiaa. Did you hum it somewhere ordinary? Today, the same pauri, opened up for its meaning. Day three hundred eighty-two.

A baby is born in a Punjabi family, and within the hour the phone is ringing. Then the doorbell. Aunties arrive with sweets. Uncles arrive with more sweets. Someone puts music on. Everyone keeps saying one word to the parents, the grandparents, anyone standing still long enough: vadhaiyan! Congratulations! It's the word for good news so big that the whole family turns up. The first pauri of Anand Sahib has that word in it. It's a party in five lines, and the guests are not who you'd expect. Today: Pauri 1, meaning: joy, mother.
screen: `A BABY IS BORN; THE PHONE RINGS.` → `AUNTIES, SWEETS, MUSIC.` → `VADHAIYAN! CONGRATULATIONS!`

segments.voice: Here's the pauri, in paraphrase. Joy has come, my mother, for I have found the True Guru. I found the True Guru with ease, and my mind rings with congratulations. The jewel-like ragas, with their families, have come to sing the Word. Sing the Word of the Lord, all you who have set it in your minds. Says Nanak, bliss has come; I have found the True Guru. Take the pieces. First, mother. The news goes to the person you'd tell first. Then sahaj, with ease. The Guru wasn't won by force. Sahaj is a big word in Sikh thought: a natural, settled ease, the opposite of straining. The joy didn't come from clawing. It came the way sleep comes. Then the party. Vaadhaaeeaa, congratulations, the same word aunties call out at a birth. And who shows up to celebrate? The ragas. In old Indian music lore, ragas were pictured with families and companions. So the pauri pictures the musical modes themselves arriving at the door like relatives, ready to sing. It's a wonderful image: joy so big the music turns up in person. Then, a turn outward. Sing the Word, all of you who've taken it in. The joy doesn't stay private. It's an invitation to everyone else in the room. And finally, back to the beginning: bliss has come. Notice what this whole pauri is not. It isn't a lecture about joy. It's a report of joy, from inside it, still breathless. That's what Guru Amar Das gives Sikhs to sing at the close of their gatherings: not an idea about bliss, but good news.
screen: `JOY HAS COME, MY MOTHER.` · `SAHAJ: FOUND WITH EASE.` · `THE RAGAS ARRIVE LIKE FAMILY.` · `SING THE WORD, ALL OF YOU.` · then, large: `JOY, MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: share one good news. Sit and breathe slowly first. Let your mind go over the last few days and find one piece of good news, any size. A friend's recovery. A finished project. A good conversation. A small win nobody noticed. Let yourself feel it again, the way the pauri does, from inside. Then, when the bell ends, tell someone. Call whoever you'd tell first. Send the message. Let the joy go out the door instead of staying in. If you pray, you can thank the Guru with Waheguru first. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 1, meaning. Joy has come, my mother: the Guru found with ease, the mind ringing with congratulations, and the ragas arriving like family to sing.
Your line: joy, mother. Today, when good news comes, yours or someone else's, say congratulations out loud and mean it, the way family does. Day three hundred eighty-two.

original.note: Gurmukhi: sahaj, natural ease and poise; in pauri 1, the Guru is found with sahaj.

trapdoor: what you thought: a line about feeling happy.
what it means: a breathless report of joy: the Guru found with ease, congratulations ringing, the ragas arriving to sing, and an invitation to everyone.
what a scholar hears: 'raag ratan parvaar pareeaa' draws on the old Indian picture of ragas with families of raginis and companions, here gathering as at a birth.

notes: Pauri 1 paraphrased in full ('satgur ta paaiaa sahaj setee man vajeeaa vaadhaaeeaa; raag ratan parvaar pareeaa sabad gaavan aaeeaa; sabado ta gaavahu haree keraa man jinee vasaaiaa'). Confirm.
Vaadhaaeeaa linked to the modern Punjabi 'vadhaiyan' (congratulations). Confirm.
Reading of 'parvaar pareeaa' as the ragas' families/companions (raginis); some commentators read pareeaa as fairies or consorts. Confirm.
Day 133 already used the 'mother / kitchen door' image; today's angle is congratulations and the ragas arriving.
Editor review (2026-10-01): cut 'every gathering' and the unsourced 'the part Sikhs know best'; the raga-family image is attributed to old music lore; the practice no longer assumes a living mother.
